name: IRF520 MOSFET driver module
description: Low-side switch module built around a Vishay/IR IRF520 N-channel power MOSFET (100 V, 9.2 A, RDS(on) 0.27 Ω at VGS = 10 V, VGS(th) 2–4 V). A GPIO high on SIG turns the MOSFET on and connects the load's V- terminal to ground, so a DC load (motor, LED strip, solenoid, pump) powered from a separate 0–24 V supply switches on. Supports PWM for dimming/speed control. Because VGS(th) can be up to 4 V, it is only partly on at 5 V logic and poorly on at 3.3 V: keep the load to about 1 A at 3.3 V logic. Sold as: common IRF520 MOSFET driver module (red PCB, green LED, 3-pin header SIG, VCC, GND; screw terminals VIN/GND for the load supply and V+/V- for the load), rated 0–24 V, up to 5 A with derating.
eli5: An electronic switch for bigger DC things like a motor or LED strip: your board says on, and the module lets the big power supply's current flow through the load.

pins.name: SIG
pins.description: Gate signal, active high: high = MOSFET on (load powered, green LED lit), low = off. Pulled down on the board so the load stays off while the GPIO floats. PWM-capable. 5 V logic drives it much harder than 3.3 V.

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: Marked VCC but not connected to anything on this module; leave it unconnected

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground, shared with the microcontroller (joined on the board to the load supply's GND terminal and the MOSFET source)

buildNotes: Wire SIG to a GPIO and GND to the microcontroller's GND. Leave the header's middle VCC pin unconnected: it goes nowhere on this board.
The load has its own supply: + of the supply to the VIN screw terminal, - to the GND screw terminal; the load goes across V+ and V-. Do not power a motor from the microcontroller's 3V3 or 5V pin.
This is a low-side switch: V- is switched to ground, V+ is always at the supply voltage. Never short V+ or V- to the microcontroller's pins.

Logic-level warning: the IRF520 is specified at VGS = 10 V and its threshold is 2–4 V. At 5 V logic it is only partly on (ProtoSupplies measured 3 A continuous giving a 56 °C tab without a heatsink); at 3.3 V logic (ESP32, Pico, Raspberry Pi) keep the load to about 1 A or use a logic-level MOSFET module (e.g. IRLZ44N, AOD4184).
Keep the load supply to 24 V or less on this module (the MOSFET itself is rated 100 V) and fit a heatsink above a few amps.
Motors, solenoids and relay coils need a flyback diode (e.g. 1N4007 or 1N5819) across the load, cathode to V+: the module has none.
PWM works for LED dimming and motor speed; keep the frequency modest (about 1 kHz) since a GPIO charges the gate slowly through the board's resistor.

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

mosfet = Pin({SIG}, Pin.OUT, value=0)  # SIG high = MOSFET on, load powered
while True:
    mosfet.value(1)
    print('LOAD ON')
    time.sleep(2)
    mosfet.value(0)
    print('LOAD OFF')
    time.sleep(2)

test.title: The MOSFET switches the load on, then off again

library.note: Passed the Sparkbench part check in simulation and matched an independent datasheet reading. Not yet tested on real hardware.
